one_liner: Concurrent C++ safetensors reader with a Python API that loads model weights to GPU faster than Hugging Face's safetensors loader.
what_it_does: Model Streamer (renamed from Run:ai Model Streamer; now at dsx-ai-factory/model-streamer) streams tensors from safetensors files on local disk, network file systems, S3, GCS or Azure Blob into a CPU buffer and yields them one by one so the caller can copy each to the GPU while later tensors are still being read. The API is a SafetensorsStreamer context manager with stream_file/stream_files and a get_tensors() iterator, plus optional tensor_names filtering and distributed streaming across ranks; it is also a vLLM load format. It is not a drop-in for safetensors.safe_open: the caller iterates (name, tensor) pairs and must clone tensors it keeps.
how_it_is_fast: Reads are split into chunks (2 MiB default on file systems, 8 MiB on object stores) and issued concurrently, overlapping storage reads with host-to-GPU copies instead of mmap page faults or a serial read. Current versions pick a file-system strategy per host from io_uring_direct, io_uring_buffered, libaio_direct and a sync_buffered thread pool (default queue depth 512 for the async engines, 16 threads for the pool), with O_DIRECT where the mount supports it. Object storage uses many parallel ranged GETs (AWS CRT client, about 10 Gbit/s per client), and distributed mode has each rank read a slice and broadcast it over NCCL.
when_to_use: Cold-start loading of large single-file or sharded safetensors checkpoints from cloud block storage (EBS GP3/IO2-class) where one reader cannot saturate the volume.
Loading weights directly from S3, GCS or Azure Blob without first copying to local disk, especially with multiple GPUs on NVLink using distributed streaming.
vLLM or PyTorch inference servers that autoscale and need short time-to-ready on x86-64 Linux.
Network file systems or virtiofs where per-filesystem queue depth tuning (RUNAI_STREAMER_FS_QUEUE_DEPTH="512,nfs=64") helps.
when_not_to_use: Mixture-of-experts checkpoints with tens of thousands of small tensors: issue #225 reports Qwen3-Next-80B (75,944 tensors, 162.7 GB) loading in 125.7 s versus 43.6 s with vLLM's default safetensors loader (2.9x slower) on a B200, from forced tensor clones and out-of-order delivery.

Warm page cache or very fast local NVMe/tmpfs: the published wins are against throttled cold EBS volumes, and InstantTensor's table shows this streamer at 9.29 s versus 1.77 s for InstantTensor on 50 GB/s storage.
Single-reader setups: at concurrency 1 it matched safetensors on GP3 (47.56 s vs 47.99 s), so the gain comes only from parallel reads.
Non-PyTorch frameworks or non-safetensors formats (docs say PyTorch only), and aarch64 via pip (pip install is documented for x86_64).

integration.form: module (pip wheel runai-model-streamer with a bundled C++ shared library; optional [s3], [gcs], [azure] backend packages)
integration.dependencies: PyTorch; libcurl4 and libssl for the C++ core; object-storage extras ship libstreamers3.so statically linked to libssl, libcrypto and libcurl; backend packages must match the core version exactly
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, built with Bazel in -c opt (-O2) inside the project devcontainer; prebuilt wheels for x86_64 Linux
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 (pip); aarch64 build config exists (-march=armv8-a+crc+crypto); io_uring and libaio engines probed at runtime with sync_buffered fallback
integration.thread_safety: not documented for sharing one SafetensorsStreamer across threads; each streamer owns its OS reader threads, which close with the context manager
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: works as a vLLM load format, but direct users replace safe_open/load_file with a streaming iterator and must clone tensors they keep

gotchas: Yielded tensors live in a reused CPU (or, in distributed mode, device staging) buffer and may be overwritten under RUNAI_STREAMER_MEMORY_LIMIT or freed when the streamer closes; clone them if you keep them (issue #230 tracks owned tensors).
Default CPU buffer cap is 40 GB in non-distributed mode; distributed streaming needs staging buffers of twice the largest tensor per device.
Concurrency must be tuned per storage: the GP3 result plateaued at concurrency 4-16 (14.43-14.34 s) because the volume's 1 GiB/s limit was hit, while S3 kept improving up to 32.
Distributed streaming is on by default for object storage to CUDA, and every rank must pass identical tensor_names; mixing S3 and file paths in one stream_files call is not allowed.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over fastsafetensors when weights sit in S3, GCS or Azure Blob or on throttled cloud block volumes and you want vLLM's built-in integration; prefer InstantTensor or fastsafetensors (GDS) for fast local NVMe or many-tensor MoE checkpoints, where this streamer was measured slower.
verified_claims_summary: First-party benchmarks.md (Model Streamer 0.6.0, vLLM 0.5.5, CUDA 12.4, AWS g5.12xlarge with one A10G, cold cache) loaded the 15 GB Meta-Llama-3-8B safetensors file in 14.34 s at concurrency 16 versus 47.99 s for the HF safetensors loader on GP3 (3.3x, derived from page data; about 1.05 GB/s versus 0.31 GB/s, derived from page data), 7.53 s versus 47 s on IO2 (6.2x, derived from page data), and 4.88 s versus Tensorizer's 37.36 s from S3; vLLM time-to-ready fell from 66.13 s to 35.08 s on GP3. These numbers predate the io_uring/libaio engines in current code, and no benchmark scripts, CPU model or build flags are published.
status_note: Actively maintained (commits through 2026-10-05, 383 stars, Apache-2.0), installable from PyPI as runai-model-streamer; the repo moved to dsx-ai-factory/model-streamer in September 2026 with the old URL redirecting.
